claim: Deep learning is emerging as a powerful approach for bioimage analysis.
source: Deep learning is emerging as a powerful approach for bioimage analysis.

source: Its use in cell tracking is limited by the scarcity of annotated data for the training of deep-learning models.
evidence: This is stated as a known limitation in the field.

claim: Annotation, training, prediction, and proofreading currently lack a unified user interface.
source: Moreover, annotation, training, prediction, and proofreading currently lack a unified user interface.

source: We present ELEPHANT, an interactive platform for 3D cell tracking that addresses these challenges by taking an incremental approach to deep learning.

claim: ELEPHANT provides an interface that seamlessly integrates cell track annotation, deep learning, prediction, and proofreading.
source: ELEPHANT provides an interface that seamlessly integrates cell track annotation, deep learning, prediction, and proofreading.

claim: ELEPHANT enables users to implement cycles of incremental learning starting from a few annotated nuclei.
source: This enables users to implement cycles of incremental learning starting from a few annotated nuclei.

claim: Successive prediction-validation cycles enrich the training data, leading to rapid improvements in tracking performance.
source: Successive prediction-validation cycles enrich the training data, leading to rapid improvements in tracking performance.

claim: The software's performance was tested against state-of-the-art methods.

claim: ELEPHANT was used to track lineages spanning the entire course of leg regeneration in a crustacean over 1 week (504 timepoints).
source: We test the software's performance against state-of-the-art methods and track lineages spanning the entire course of leg regeneration in a crustacean over 1 week (504 timepoints).

evidence: This is a summary claim about the software's performance.

source: Recent progress in deep learning has led to significant advances in bioimage analysis (Moen et al., 2019; Ouyang et al., 2018; Weigert et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to relevant literature.

claim: Deep learning is adaptable to a variety of datasets once an appropriate model architecture is selected and trained with adequate data.
source: As deep learning is data-driven, it is adaptable to a variety of datasets once an appropriate model architecture is selected and trained with adequate data (Moen et al., 2019).

claim: The preparation of new training data is laborious.
source: First, pre-trained models can be inadequate for new tasks and the preparation of new training data is laborious.
evidence: This is stated as a known challenge in the field.

claim: The quality and quantity of training data are crucial for the performance of deep learning.
source: Because the quality and quantity of the training data are crucial for the performance of deep learning, users must invest significant time and effort in annotation at the start of the project (Moen et al., 2019).

claim: Users must invest significant time and effort in annotation at the start of deep learning projects.
source: Because the quality and quantity of the training data are crucial for the performance of deep learning, users must invest significant time and effort in annotation at the start of the project (Moen et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation.

claim: An interactive user interface for deep learning in the context of cell tracking is lacking.
source: Second, an interactive user interface for deep learning, especially in the context of cell tracking, is lacking (Kok et al., 2020; Wen et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: Deep learning applications are often limited by accessibility to computing power (high-end GPU).
source: Third, deep learning applications are often limited by accessibility to computing power (high-end GPU).
evidence: This is stated as a known limitation.

claim: ELEPHANT is a web-friendly platform for cell tracking.
source: We have addressed these challenges by establishing ELEPHANT (Efficient learning using sparse human annotations for nuclear tracking), an interactive web-friendly platform for cell tracking, which seamlessly integrates manual annotation with deep learning and proofreading of the results.
evidence: This describes a feature of the software.

claim: ELEPHANT implements two algorithms optimized for incremental deep learning using sparse annotations.
source: ELEPHANT implements two algorithms optimized for incremental deep learning using sparse annotations, one for detecting nuclei in 3D and a second for linking these nuclei across timepoints in 4D image datasets.
evidence: This describes the algorithms implemented in the software.

claim: One ELEPHANT algorithm is for detecting nuclei in 3D.
source: ELEPHANT implements two algorithms optimized for incremental deep learning using sparse annotations, one for detecting nuclei in 3D and a second for linking these nuclei across timepoints in 4D image datasets.
evidence: This describes one of the algorithms.

claim: One ELEPHANT algorithm is for linking nuclei across timepoints in 4D image datasets.
source: ELEPHANT implements two algorithms optimized for incremental deep learning using sparse annotations, one for detecting nuclei in 3D and a second for linking these nuclei across timepoints in 4D image datasets.
evidence: This describes one of the algorithms.

claim: Incremental learning allows models to be trained in a stepwise fashion on a given dataset, starting from sparse annotations that are incrementally enriched by human proofreading.
source: Incremental learning allows models to be trained in a stepwise fashion on a given dataset, starting from sparse annotations that are incrementally enriched by human proofreading, leading to a rapid increase in performance (Figure 1).
evidence: This describes the incremental learning approach, with reference to Figure 1.

claim: Incremental learning leads to a rapid increase in performance.
source: Incremental learning allows models to be trained in a stepwise fashion on a given dataset, starting from sparse annotations that are incrementally enriched by human proofreading, leading to a rapid increase in performance (Figure 1).
evidence: This is a claim about the outcome of incremental learning, with reference to Figure 1.

claim: ELEPHANT is implemented as an extension of Mastodon.
source: ELEPHANT is implemented as an extension of Mastodon (https://github.com/mastodon-sc/mastodon; Mastodon Science, 2021), an open-source framework for large-scale tracking deployed in Fiji (Schindelin et al., 2012).
evidence: This describes the software implementation.

claim: Mastodon is an open-source framework for large-scale tracking deployed in Fiji.
source: ELEPHANT is implemented as an extension of Mastodon (https://github.com/mastodon-sc/mastodon; Mastodon Science, 2021), an open-source framework for large-scale tracking deployed in Fiji (Schindelin et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: ELEPHANT implements a client-server architecture.
source: It implements a client-server architecture, in which the server provides a deep learning environment equipped with sufficient GPU (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This describes the software architecture, with reference to a figure.

claim: The ELEPHANT server provides a deep learning environment equipped with sufficient GPU.
source: It implements a client-server architecture, in which the server provides a deep learning environment equipped with sufficient GPU (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This describes the server component, with reference to a figure.

claim: ELEPHANT employs the tracking-by-detection paradigm.
source: ELEPHANT employs the tracking-by-detection paradigm (Maška et al., 2014), which involves initially the detection of nuclei in 3D and subsequently their linking over successive timepoints to generate tracks.
evidence: This describes the tracking approach, supported by a citation.

claim: The tracking-by-detection paradigm involves initially the detection of nuclei in 3D and subsequently their linking over successive timepoints to generate tracks.
source: ELEPHANT employs the tracking-by-detection paradigm (Maška et al., 2014), which involves initially the detection of nuclei in 3D and subsequently their linking over successive timepoints to generate tracks.
evidence: This describes the tracking paradigm, supported by a citation.

claim: In ELEPHANT, nuclei are represented as ellipsoids using the data model of Mastodon.
source: In both steps, the nuclei are represented as ellipsoids, using the data model of Mastodon (Figure 2A and Figure 4A).
evidence: This describes the data representation, with reference to figures.

claim: Ellipsoids are used for annotation because they allow rapid and efficient training and prediction compared with more complex shapes.
source: We use ellipsoids for annotation because ellipsoids allow rapid and efficient training and prediction, compared with more complex shapes.
evidence: This explains the rationale for using ellipsoids.

claim: Rapid and efficient training and prediction is essential for interactive deep learning.
source: This is essential for interactive deep learning.
evidence: This explains why rapid training is important.

claim: In the detection phase, voxels are labelled as background, nucleus center, or nucleus periphery, or left unlabelled.
source: In the detection phase, voxels are labelled as background, nucleus center or nucleus periphery, or left unlabelled (Figure 2A, top right).
evidence: This describes the labeling scheme, with reference to a figure.

claim: The nucleus center and nucleus periphery labels are generated by the annotation of nuclei.
source: The nucleus center and nucleus periphery labels are generated by the annotation of nuclei, and the background can be annotated either manually or by intensity thresholding.
evidence: This describes how labels are generated.

claim: The background can be annotated either manually or by intensity thresholding.
source: The nucleus center and nucleus periphery labels are generated by the annotation of nuclei, and the background can be annotated either manually or by intensity thresholding.
evidence: This describes how background is annotated.

claim: Sparse annotations (e.g. of a few nuclei in a single timepoint) are sufficient to start training.
source: Sparse annotations (e.g. of a few nuclei in a single timepoint) are sufficient to start training.
evidence: This is a key claim about the data requirements.

claim: A U-Net convolutional neural network is trained on labels to generate voxel-wise probability maps for background, nucleus center, or nucleus periphery.
source: A U-Net convolutional neural network (U-Net CNN; Cicek et al., 2016; Ronneberger et al., 2015, Figure 2—figure supplement 1) is then trained on these labels (ignoring the unlabelled voxels) to generate voxel-wise probability maps for background, nucleus center, or nucleus periphery, across the entire image dataset (Figure 2A, bottom right).
evidence: This describes the neural network training, supported by citations and figure references.

claim: Unlabelled voxels are ignored during U-Net training.
source: A U-Net convolutional neural network (U-Net CNN; Cicek et al., 2016; Ronneberger et al., 2015, Figure 2—figure supplement 1) is then trained on these labels (ignoring the unlabelled voxels) to generate voxel-wise probability maps for background, nucleus center, or nucleus periphery, across the entire image dataset (Figure 2A, bottom right).
evidence: This describes a detail of the training process.

claim: Post-processing on probability maps yields predictions of nuclei which are available for visual inspection and proofreading.
source: Post-processing on these probability maps yields predictions of nuclei which are available for visual inspection and proofreading (validation or rejection of each predicted nucleus) by the user (Figure 2A, bottom left).
evidence: This describes the post-processing and proofreading workflow, with reference to a figure.

claim: Human-computer interaction is facilitated by color coding of annotated nuclei as predicted (green), accepted (cyan), or rejected (magenta).
source: Human-computer interaction is facilitated by color coding of the annotated nuclei as predicted (green), accepted (cyan), or rejected (magenta) (see Figure 2—figure supplement 2), based on the proofreading.
evidence: This describes the user interface feature, with reference to a figure.

claim: The cycles of training and prediction are rapid because only a small amount of training data are added each time (in the order of seconds).
source: The cycles of training and prediction are rapid because only a small amount of training data are added each time (in the order of seconds, see Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This describes the speed of the workflow, with reference to supplementary data.

claim: Users can enrich the annotations by proofreading the output almost simultaneously, enabling incremental training of the model in an efficient manner.
source: As a result, users can enrich the annotations by proofreading the output almost simultaneously, enabling incremental training of the model in an efficient manner.
evidence: This describes the benefit of rapid training cycles.

claim: The detection performance of ELEPHANT was evaluated on diverse image datasets capturing embryonic development of C. elegans, leg regeneration in P. hawaiensis, human intestinal organoids, and human breast carcinoma cells.
source: We evaluated the detection performance of ELEPHANT on diverse image datasets capturing the embryonic development of Caenorhabditis elegans (CE1), leg regeneration in the crustacean Parhyale hawaiensis (PH), human intestinal organoids (ORG1 and ORG2) and human breast carcinoma cells (MDA231) by confocal or light sheet microscopy (Figure 3A–E).
evidence: This describes the evaluation datasets, with reference to figures.

claim: A generic model pre-trained with various annotated image datasets was tested on multiple datasets.
source: First, we tested the performance of a generic model that had been pre-trained with various annotated image datasets (Figure 3A–E top).
evidence: This describes the first evaluation step, with reference to figures.

claim: Annotating 3–10 additional nuclei or cells on each test dataset and re-training the model resulted in greatly improved detection performance.
source: We then annotated 3–10 additional nuclei or cells on each test dataset (Figure 3A–E middle) and re-trained the model. This resulted in greatly improved detection performance (Figure 3A–E), showing that a very modest amount of additional training on a given dataset can yield rapid improvements in performance.
evidence: This describes the fine-tuning experiment and its results, with reference to figures.

claim: A very modest amount of additional training on a given dataset can yield rapid improvements in performance.
source: This resulted in greatly improved detection performance (Figure 3A–E), showing that a very modest amount of additional training on a given dataset can yield rapid improvements in performance.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the fine-tuning experiment.

claim: Sparsely trained ELEPHANT detection models have a comparable performance to state-of-the-art software.
source: We find that sparsely trained ELEPHANT detection models have a comparable performance to state-of-the-art software (Figure 3—figure supplement 1) and fully trained ELEPHANT models outperform most tracking software (Table 1).
evidence: This is a comparison claim supported by figure and table references.

claim: Fully trained ELEPHANT models outperform most tracking software.
source: We find that sparsely trained ELEPHANT detection models have a comparable performance to state-of-the-art software (Figure 3—figure supplement 1) and fully trained ELEPHANT models outperform most tracking software (Table 1).
evidence: This is a comparison claim supported by a table reference.

claim: Training with sparse annotations did not cause overfitting of the data in the detection model.
source: We also investigated whether training with sparse annotations could cause overfitting of the data in the detection model, by training the detection model using sparse annotations in dataset CE1 and calculating the loss values using a second, unseen but similar dataset (see Materials and methods). The training and validation learning curves did not show any signs of overfitting even after a large amount of training (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This describes an overfitting investigation, with reference to a figure.

claim: The trained model could detect nuclei with high precision and recall both on partially seen data (CE1) and unseen data (CE2).
source: The trained model could detect nuclei with high precision and recall both on partially seen data (CE1) and unseen data (CE2).
evidence: This describes the generalization performance of the model.

claim: A detection model that has been pre-trained with diverse image datasets is available to users as a starting point for tracking on new image data.
source: A detection model that has been pre-trained with diverse image datasets is available to users as a starting point for tracking on new image data (see Materials and methods).
evidence: This describes a resource provided to users.

claim: Nearest neighbor approaches for tracking nuclei over time perform poorly in challenging datasets when cells are dividing.
source: In the linking phase, we found that nearest neighbor approaches for tracking nuclei over time (Crocker and Grier, 1996) perform poorly in challenging datasets when the cells are dividing; hence we turned to optical flow modeling to improve linking (Amat et al., 2013; Horn and Schunck, 1981; Lucas and Kanade, 1981).
evidence: This describes a limitation of nearest neighbor approaches, supported by citations.

claim: Optical flow modeling was used to improve linking.
source: In the linking phase, we found that nearest neighbor approaches for tracking nuclei over time (Crocker and Grier, 1996) perform poorly in challenging datasets when the cells are dividing; hence we turned to optical flow modeling to improve linking (Amat et al., 2013; Horn and Schunck, 1981; Lucas and Kanade, 1981).
evidence: This describes the approach taken to improve linking, supported by citations.

claim: A second U-Net CNN, optimized for optical flow estimation, is trained on manually generated/validated links between nuclei in successive timepoints.
source: A second U-Net CNN, optimized for optical flow estimation (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), is trained on manually generated/validated links between nuclei in successive timepoints (Figure 4A, top left).
evidence: This describes the flow model training, with reference to figures.

claim: Unlabelled voxels are ignored during flow model training, hence training can be performed on sparse linking annotations.
source: Unlabelled voxels are ignored, hence training can be performed on sparse linking annotations.
evidence: This describes a feature of the flow model training.

claim: The flow model is used to generate voxel-wise 3D flow maps, representing predicted x, y and z displacements over time.
source: The flow model is used to generate voxel-wise 3D flow maps, representing predicted x, y and z displacements over time (Figure 4A, bottom right), which are then combined with nearest neighbor linking to predict links between the detected nuclei (see Materials and methods).
evidence: This describes the output of the flow model, with reference to a figure.

claim: Flow maps are combined with nearest neighbor linking to predict links between detected nuclei.
source: The flow model is used to generate voxel-wise 3D flow maps, representing predicted x, y and z displacements over time (Figure 4A, bottom right), which are then combined with nearest neighbor linking to predict links between the detected nuclei (see Materials and methods).
evidence: This describes how flow predictions are used for linking.

claim: Users proofread the linking results to finalize the tracks and to update the labels for the next iteration of training.
source: Users proofread the linking results to finalize the tracks and to update the labels for the next iteration of training (Figure 4A, bottom left).
evidence: This describes the proofreading workflow, with reference to a figure.

claim: The linking performance of ELEPHANT was evaluated using C. elegans embryonic development datasets and P. hawaiensis limb regeneration datasets.
source: We evaluated the linking performance of ELEPHANT using two types of 4D confocal microscopy datasets in which nuclei were visualized by fluorescent markers: the first type of dataset captures the embryonic development of Caenorhabditis elegans (CE datasets), which has been used in previous studies to benchmark tracking methods (Murray et al., 2008; Ulman et al., 2017), and the second type captures limb regeneration in Parhyale hawaiensis (PH dataset, imaging adapted from Alwes et al., 2016), which presents greater challenges for image analysis (see below, Figure 5—video 1).
evidence: This describes the evaluation datasets, supported by citations.

claim: The CE datasets have been used in previous studies to benchmark tracking methods.
source: the first type of dataset captures the embryonic development of Caenorhabditis elegans (CE datasets), which has been used in previous studies to benchmark tracking methods (Murray et al., 2008; Ulman et al., 2017)
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: The PH dataset presents greater challenges for image analysis than the CE datasets.
source: and the second type captures limb regeneration in Parhyale hawaiensis (PH dataset, imaging adapted from Alwes et al., 2016), which presents greater challenges for image analysis (see below, Figure 5—video 1).
evidence: This is stated and elaborated on later in the manuscript.

claim: Fewer than 10 annotated nuclei are sufficient to initiate a virtuous cycle of training, prediction, and proofreading for both CE and PH datasets.
source: For both types of dataset, we find that fewer than 10 annotated nuclei are sufficient to initiate a virtuous cycle of training, prediction, and proofreading, which efficiently yields cell tracks and validated cell lineages in highly dynamic tissues.
evidence: This is a key finding about data requirements.

claim: Interactive cycles of manual annotation, deep learning, and proofreading on ELEPHANT reduce the time required to detect and validate nuclei.
source: Interactive cycles of manual annotation, deep learning, and proofreading on ELEPHANT reduce the time required to detect and validate nuclei (Figure 2B).
evidence: This describes a benefit of the workflow, with reference to a figure.

claim: On the CE1 dataset, a complete cell lineage was built over 195 timepoints, from scratch, using ELEPHANT's semi-automated workflow.
source: On the CE1 dataset, a complete cell lineage was built over 195 timepoints, from scratch, using ELEPHANT's semi-automated workflow (Figure 4B).
evidence: This describes a specific application result, with reference to a figure.

claim: The detection model for CE1 was trained incrementally starting from sparse annotations (four nuclei) on the first timepoint.
source: The detection model was trained incrementally starting from sparse annotations (four nuclei) on the first timepoint.
evidence: This describes the training approach for CE1.

claim: On the CE1 dataset, linking could be performed using the nearest neighbor algorithm without flow modeling and manual proofreading.
source: On this dataset, linking could be performed using the nearest neighbor algorithm (without flow modeling) and manual proofreading.
evidence: This describes the linking approach for CE1.

claim: 23,829 nuclei were annotated in less than 8 hr on the CE1 dataset (across 195 timepoints), of which ~2% were manually annotated (483 nuclei) and the remaining nuclei were collected by validating predictions.
source: In this way, we were able to annotate in less than 8 hr a total of 23,829 nuclei (across 195 timepoints), of which ~ 2% were manually annotated (483 nuclei) and the remaining nuclei were collected by validating predictions of the deep-learning model.
evidence: This provides quantitative data on the annotation effort.

claim: Cell tracking can be accelerated by starting from models trained on image data with similar characteristics.
source: Although ELEPHANT works efficiently without prior training, cell tracking can be accelerated by starting from models trained on image data with similar characteristics.
evidence: This is a general claim about transfer learning.

claim: A pre-trained model from CE2 allowed detection of nuclei in CE1 much more rapidly and effortlessly than with an untrained model.
source: To illustrate this, we used nuclear annotations in a separate dataset, CE2, to train a model for detection, which was then applied to CE1. This pre-trained model allowed us to detect nuclei in CE1 much more rapidly and effortlessly than with an untrained model (Figure 2B, blue versus orange curves).
evidence: This demonstrates the benefit of pre-training, with reference to a figure.

claim: ELEPHANT models with assistance of flow-based interpolation outperformed state-of-the-art tracking algorithms in detection (DET) and tracking (TRA) metrics on the Cell Tracking Challenge.
source: For benchmarking, the detection and linkage models trained with the annotations from the CE1 and CE2 lineage trees were then tested on unseen datasets with similar characteristics (without proofreading), as part of the Cell Tracking Challenge (Maška et al., 2014; Ulman et al., 2017). In this test, our models with assistance of flow-based interpolation (see Materials and methods) outperformed state-of-the-art tracking algorithms (Magnusson et al., 2015; Scherr et al., 2020) in detection (DET) and tracking (TRA) metrics (Table 1).
evidence: This is a benchmarking result, supported by citations and table reference.

claim: ELEPHANT performs less well in segmentation (SEG) than some state-of-the-art methods, probably due to the use of ellipsoids to approximate nuclear shapes.
source: ELEPHANT performs less well in segmentation (SEG), probably due to the use of ellipsoids to approximate nuclear shapes.
evidence: This is a limitation acknowledged by the authors, with a proposed explanation.

claim: The PH dataset presents challenges such as larger variations in the shape, intensity, and distribution of nuclei, lower temporal resolution, and more noise.
source: The PH dataset presents greater challenges for image analysis, such as larger variations in the shape, intensity, and distribution of nuclei, lower temporal resolution, and more noise (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This describes the characteristics of the PH dataset, with reference to a figure.

claim: ELEPHANT allowed continued training of models through visual feedback from the user to address challenges in the PH dataset.
source: ELEPHANT has allowed us to grapple with these issues by supporting the continued training of the models through visual feedback from the user (annotation of missed nuclei, validation and rejection of predictions).
evidence: This describes how ELEPHANT addresses the PH dataset challenges.

claim: Over 260,000 nuclei were annotated and validated in the PH dataset across 504 timepoints spanning 168 hr of imaging using ELEPHANT.
source: Using ELEPHANT, we annotated and validated over 260,000 nuclei in this dataset, across 504 timepoints spanning 168 hr of imaging.
evidence: This provides quantitative data on the annotation effort for PH.

claim: The conventional nearest neighbor approach was inadequate for linking in the PH dataset, resulting in many errors in the lineage trees.
source: We observed that the conventional nearest neighbor approach was inadequate for linking in the PH dataset, resulting in many errors in the lineage trees (Figure 4C).
evidence: This describes a limitation of nearest neighbor linking for PH, with reference to a figure.

claim: The inadequacy of nearest neighbor linking in PH is likely due to the lower temporal resolution (20 min in PH, versus 1–2 min in CE) and the fact that daughter nuclei often show large displacements at the end of mitosis.
source: This is likely due to the lower temporal resolution in this dataset (20 min in PH, versus 1–2 min in CE) and the fact that daughter nuclei often show large displacements at the end of mitosis.
evidence: This provides an explanation for the linking challenges in PH.

claim: Optical flow was trained using 1,162 validated links collected from 10 timepoints (including 18 links for 9 cell divisions) in the PH dataset.
source: We trained optical flow using 1,162 validated links collected from 10 timepoints (including 18 links for 9 cell divisions).
evidence: This describes the training data for the flow model in PH.

claim: Sparse annotations were sufficient to generate 3D optical flow predictions for the entire PH dataset.
source: These sparse annotations were sufficient to generate 3D optical flow predictions for the entire dataset (Figure 4—video 1), which significantly improved the linking performance (Figure 4C, Supplementary file 2)
evidence: This demonstrates the effectiveness of sparse training for flow prediction.

claim: Optical flow predictions significantly improved the linking performance in the PH dataset.
source: These sparse annotations were sufficient to generate 3D optical flow predictions for the entire dataset (Figure 4—video 1), which significantly improved the linking performance (Figure 4C, Supplementary file 2): the number of false positive and false negative links decreased by ~57% (from 2093 to 905) and ~32% (from 1991 to 1349), respectively, among a total of 259,071 links.
evidence: This provides quantitative evidence of improvement, with reference to figures and supplementary files.

claim: The number of false positive links decreased by ~57% (from 2093 to 905) with optical flow in the PH dataset.
source: the number of false positive and false negative links decreased by ~57% (from 2093 to 905) and ~32% (from 1991 to 1349), respectively, among a total of 259,071 links.
evidence: This provides specific quantitative results.

claim: The number of false negative links decreased by ~32% (from 1991 to 1349) with optical flow in the PH dataset.
source: the number of false positive and false negative links decreased by ~57% (from 2093 to 905) and ~32% (from 1991 to 1349), respectively, among a total of 259,071 links.
evidence: This provides specific quantitative results.

claim: 109 complete and fully validated cell lineage trees were reconstructed encompassing the duration of leg regeneration in Parhyale, each lineage spanning a period of ~1 week (504 timepoints).
source: By applying ELEPHANT's human-in-the-loop semi-automated workflow, we succeeded in reconstructing 109 complete and fully validated cell lineage trees encompassing the duration of leg regeneration in Parhyale, each lineage spanning a period of ~1 week (504 timepoints, Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This describes a major result of the study, with reference to a figure.

claim: Analysis and visualization modules implemented in Mastodon and ELEPHANT allowed capturing the distribution of cell divisions across time and space.
source: Using analysis and visualization modules implemented in Mastodon and ELEPHANT, we could capture the distribution of cell divisions across time and space (Figure 5A) and produce a fate map of the regenerating leg of Parhyale (Figure 5B).
evidence: This describes the analysis capabilities, with reference to figures.

claim: A fate map of the regenerating leg of Parhyale was produced using ELEPHANT.
source: Using analysis and visualization modules implemented in Mastodon and ELEPHANT, we could capture the distribution of cell divisions across time and space (Figure 5A) and produce a fate map of the regenerating leg of Parhyale (Figure 5B).
evidence: This describes a biological result, with reference to a figure.

claim: The analysis that would have required several months of manual annotation was achieved in ~1 month of interactive cell tracking in ELEPHANT, without prior training.
source: This analysis, which would have required several months of manual annotation, was achieved in ~1 month of interactive cell tracking in ELEPHANT, without prior training.
evidence: This provides a comparison of time investment.

claim: Applying the best performing models to new data could improve tracking efficiency even further.
source: Applying the best performing models to new data could improve tracking efficiency even further.
evidence: This is a speculation about future improvements.

claim: The PH dataset was obtained by imaging a regenerating T4 leg of the crustacean Parhyale hawaiensis.
source: The PH dataset (dataset li13) was obtained by imaging a regenerating T4 leg of the crustacean Parhyale hawaiensis, based on the method described by Alwes et al., 2016; Figure 5—video 1.
evidence: This describes the source of the PH dataset, supported by a citation.

claim: The imaging for the PH dataset was carried out on a transgenic animal carrying the Mi(3xP3> DsRed; PhHS> H2B-mRFPRuby) construct.
source: The imaging was carried out on a transgenic animal carrying the Mi(3xP3> DsRed; PhHS> H2B-mRFPRuby) construct (Wolff et al., 2018), in which nuclear-localised mRFPRuby fluorescent protein is expressed in all cells following heat-shock.
evidence: This describes the experimental setup, supported by a citation.

claim: In the transgenic animal used for PH imaging, nuclear-localised mRFPRuby fluorescent protein is expressed in all cells following heat-shock.
source: The imaging was carried out on a transgenic animal carrying the Mi(3xP3> DsRed; PhHS> H2B-mRFPRuby) construct (Wolff et al., 2018), in which nuclear-localised mRFPRuby fluorescent protein is expressed in all cells following heat-shock.
evidence: This describes the transgenic construct function.

claim: The leg for PH imaging was amputated at the distal end of the carpus.
source: The leg was amputated at the distal end of the carpus.
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure.

claim: Continuous live imaging over a period of 1 week was performed on a Zeiss LSM 800 confocal microscope for the PH dataset.
source: Following the amputation, continuous live imaging over a period of 1 week was performed on a Zeiss LSM 800 confocal microscope equipped with a Plan-Apochromat 20 x/0.8 M27 objective (Zeiss 420650-9901-000), in a temperature control chamber set to 26 °C.
evidence: This describes the imaging setup.

claim: Heat-shocks (45 minutes at 37 °C) were applied 24 hr prior to the amputation, and 65 and 138 hr post-amputation for the PH dataset.
source: Heat-shocks (45 minutes at 37 °C) were applied 24 hr prior to the amputation, and 65 and 138 hr post-amputation.
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure.

claim: Every 20 min a stack of 11 optical sections was recorded for the PH dataset, with a z step of 2.48 microns.
source: Every 20 min we recorded a stack of 11 optical sections, with a z step of 2.48 microns.
